title: Ratios, Rates, Proportions and Units, Part 2: Medium and Hard Problems

beats.say: In part one, we used a unit rate and a proportion to scale a price. A proportion needs the same quantities in the same order.
In this video, we split a total using a ratio, and then convert units through a long chain of conversion factors.
Medium example. The ratio of red marbles to blue marbles is seven to three. There are fifty marbles in total. How many marbles are blue?

card.sub: 50 marbles in total. How many blue?

beats.say: In a ratio of seven to three, the red marbles are seven k and the blue marbles are three k, for some number k. Together they make fifty.
Add the two parts. Seven k plus three k equals fifty, because the parts together are the total.
Seven k plus three k is ten k, because we are adding the numbers in front of the same letter.
Divide both sides by ten. Fifty divided by ten is five. So each part of the ratio is worth five marbles.
The red marbles are seven times five, which is thirty-five. Each part of the ratio is worth five marbles.
The blue marbles are three times five, which is fifteen. So fifteen marbles are blue. Notice that the ratio parts are seven and three, but the actual numbers are thirty-five and fifteen.
Check the total. Thirty-five plus fifteen is fifty, which matches the problem.
Hard example. A leaky faucet drips six milliliters every fifteen seconds. How many liters does it waste in one day? One liter equals one thousand milliliters.
This is a unit conversion chain. We start with milliliters per second and multiply by conversion fractions until we reach liters per day.
First, there are sixty seconds in a minute. Multiplying by sixty seconds over one minute cancels the seconds, and gives us minutes.
Next, there are sixty minutes in an hour. This cancels the minutes and gives us hours.
Then, there are twenty-four hours in a day. This cancels the hours and gives us days.
Finally, one liter is one thousand milliliters. Multiplying by one liter over one thousand milliliters cancels milliliters and gives liters.
Write the whole chain in one line. Six over fifteen is the drip rate in milliliters per second, and the remaining numbers convert the units.
Six divided by fifteen is zero point four. So the faucet wastes zero point four milliliters every second.

Sixty times sixty times twenty-four is eighty-six thousand four hundred, the number of seconds in a day. Multiplying by zero point four gives thirty-four thousand five hundred sixty milliliters per day.
Divide by one thousand to convert milliliters to liters. Thirty-four thousand five hundred sixty divided by one thousand is thirty-four point five six.

Check another way. A day has eighty-six thousand four hundred seconds, and zero point four times that is thirty-four thousand five hundred sixty milliliters. In liters, that is thirty-four point five six.
To recap. In a ratio, the quantities are multiples of a common k, and the parts add to the total.
beats.item: Ratio parts are multiples of k

beats.say: For unit conversions, write a chain of fractions equal to one, so that every unwanted unit cancels.
Check by converting a different way. In the next video, we look at common traps and the fast way with Desmos.
